html:
El Paraíso is a large stone-built ceremonial complex of the Late Preceramic period, in the Chillón River valley near the coast just north of modern Lima, Peru. It was built around 2000 BCE and is one of the largest monuments of its time in the Americas.

Its builders raised several mound-like buildings of stone, with plastered rooms, around a large open plaza in a U shape, an early example of a plan later common in Peruvian temples. They had no pottery yet. They ate fish and shellfish from the sea and grew cotton, squash and beans; cotton gave them fishing nets and cloth.

It belongs to the same coastal tradition as Caral and the other Norte Chico sites, and comes before Chavín. The map keeps it to 500 BCE, though the site itself was in use for a shorter time. Part of one mound was destroyed by developers in 2013.
